mission: A University of Oxford initiative (at the Oxford Martin School) working on frontier, international, China and technical AI governance, including a Hardware AI Governance Lab and the first Technical AI Governance DPhil studentships. It aims to support decision-makers in industry, government and civil society. Also covered by the policy group's entry (shared logo file logos/aigi.jpg). Founding year approximate.

key_work.title: Gold-Standard AI Risk-Management Framework: A Research Agenda (talk)
key_work.plain_summary: Director Robert Trager outlines what a best-practice risk-management framework for frontier AI should contain.

key_work.title: Technical AI Governance programme
key_work.plain_summary: Research and DPhil training on the technical tools — such as hardware verification — that make AI rules enforceable.

key_work.title: Verification for International AI Governance
key_work.plain_summary: Explains how countries could check each other's compliance with AI agreements; verifying data-centre AI development looks feasible within a few years with serious effort.

key_work.title: The Annual AI Governance Report 2025: Steering the Future of AI
key_work.plain_summary: A yearly overview of how AI governance developed and where it should go next.

key_work.title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability
key_work.plain_summary: Warns that a model's written 'reasoning' may not truly reflect how it reached an answer, so it should not be treated as an explanation.

key_work.title: International Governance of Civilian AI: A Jurisdictional Certification Approach
key_work.plain_summary: Proposes an International AI Organization that certifies countries' AI oversight, with trade restrictions on AI-embodying goods from uncertified jurisdictions.

key_work.title: In Which Areas of Technical AI Safety Could Geopolitical Rivals Cooperate?
key_work.plain_summary: Identifies safety research topics where the US and China could work together without giving away strategic advantage.

key_work.title: Open Problems in Frontier AI Risk Management
key_work.plain_summary: A 'living' map of unsolved problems in managing frontier AI risk, for researchers and policymakers.

people.role: Senior Researcher; lead of technical safety governance

warnings.text: 'AI also poses substantial risks both from unintended consequences and from deliberate misuse by malicious actors' (homepage).
Rigorous work on AI's social and political challenges 'remains sparse' even though they are quickly becoming one of the world's most urgent problems (homepage).
AI poses substantial risks from unintended consequences and from deliberate misuse.
Chain-of-thought explanations can be unfaithful, giving false confidence about what models are doing.
International AI agreements are hard to verify, and states differ greatly in governance style and ideology.

recommendations.text: Combine technical AI research with deep policy analysis to inform decision-makers (mission).
Build international institutions and verification mechanisms for governing advanced AI (Trager's work).
Invest now in technical verification methods for international AI agreements.
Develop international institutions (e.g. jurisdictional certification) for advanced AI.
Train technical-and-policy 'bridge' researchers for governments and industry.
